meta.label: Crowdfunding platforms
tradeoffLabels: more of what backers give reaches the campaign
backer has recourse if a campaign fails to deliver or misuses funds
meta.attribution: Fee figures come from each platform's own published fee, pricing or help-center page, read directly, plus the FTC's 2015 press release on a Kickstarter creator settlement and the SEC's Regulation Crowdfunding escrow rule, both read from the primary document rather than a summary of it. Fee figures are generally each platform's stated US rate; several vary by country, campaign type or whether a donor opts to cover the processing cost, and more than one changed its fee structure within the last year: Indiegogo moved to fixed funding and updated its fee page in October 2025, and Patreon moved creators who publish a new page to a flat 10% plan in August 2025. Check the linked page before relying on a number here. The buyer_protection score describes a guarantee, vetting process or legal escrow requirement the platform states for itself, not an independent audit of how often a claim is honored in practice; where no such statement was found, the cell is left empty rather than guessed. Reward-based platforms such as Kickstarter, Indiegogo and Experiment only collect money if a campaign reaches its funding goal, but none of them guarantee that a funded project delivers; the clearest documented case of what happens when one does not is the FTC's 2015 settlement with the creator of a failed Kickstarter board game campaign, brought against the creator, not the platform. Equity crowdfunding under SEC Regulation Crowdfunding works differently: funds must sit in escrow with a bank or broker-dealer and are released to the company only once the raise closes, and an investor can cancel for any reason up to 48 hours before the deadline. Two platforms restructure the money question itself: DonorsChoose never releases cash, it buys and ships the requested classroom materials directly, and Zeffy passes on 100% of every donation and covers its own costs from a separate voluntary tip. Giving directly to a specific charity through its own donation page, see Causes to support and Charities by cause, avoids a crowdfunding platform's cut entirely; it just is not a comparison of crowdfunding platforms, so it is not scored here. Equity crowdfunding is covered in both regions it is offered to retail investors here: US funding portals (StartEngine, Wefunder, Republic) are checked against the eCFR or Cornell Law's copy of the Regulation Crowdfunding escrow rule, FINRA's list of the funding portals it regulates and the SEC's investor bulletin, and UK platforms (Republic Europe, formerly Seedrs, and Crowdcube) against each firm's record on the FCA Financial Services Register and the FCA Handbook's rules for promoting restricted mass market investments, COBS 4.12A. The UK has no equivalent of the US escrow-until-target rule, so UK equity platforms score lower on buyer protection. Crowdcube's own fee pages could not be opened for this check, so it has no fee score. Suggest changes via Contribute.

criteria.label: Low platform and payment fees, more of what is given reaches the campaign
Backer or donor has recourse if a campaign fails to deliver or misuses funds
Easy for a backer or donor to give from where they are, without extra paperwork or limits

products.name: Kickstarter
products.description: A reward-based crowdfunding platform for creative and product projects. Campaigns are all-or-nothing: nobody is charged unless the funding goal is met, but once a project is funded there is no guarantee it will ship.

fees.note: Kickstarter's own fees page states that if a project is successfully funded, it collects Kickstarter's 5% fee plus payment processing fees of between 3% and 5%: 3% + $0.30 per pledge for standard pledges, or a discounted micropledge fee of 5% + $0.08 per pledge for pledges under $10. If funding is not successful, there are no fees.

buyer_protection.note: Kickstarter's help center article 'Does Kickstarter issue refunds?' (updated August 2026) opens: 'Kickstarter is not a store and we do not issue refunds.' A backer can cancel a pledge while a project is live, but once a funded project has ended and collection has started, a refund has to be requested from the creator, who may decline because 'creators are responsible for issuing refunds, and Kickstarter is not involved in this process.' The creator's obligation is to finish the work and deliver rewards to the best of their abilities, with no platform guarantee behind it. The clearest documented consequence of a failed delivery remains the FTC's 2015 settlement with Erik Chevalier, creator of the Kickstarter board game The Doom That Came to Atlantic City, an order against the creator rather than Kickstarter: recourse for a failed project runs against the creator.

accessibility.note: Kickstarter's help center states project creation is currently available only to eligible creators in 25 listed countries (including the US, UK, and most of the EU) and that residents outside those countries cannot launch projects. Backing a project has no such list; anyone able to pledge by card can back an eligible project.

links.label: FTC: crowdfunding project creator settles charges of deception

products.name: Indiegogo
products.description: A reward-based crowdfunding platform for products, causes and creative projects, now owned by Gamefound. Its October 2025 fee update moved new campaigns to a fixed funding model that only charges fees on successfully funded projects.

fees.note: Indiegogo's fees article states it charges a platform fee of 5% of the collected amount, plus payment processing of a fixed fee in the project currency plus 0.2 per transaction (about 3% + $0.20 in USD). Its own worked example shows a $10,000 raise pays a $500 platform fee and a $320 processing fee, netting a $9,180 payout, and the article states that if a project does not reach its goal, no fees at all are charged, including processing fees.

buyer_protection.note: Since Indiegogo moved onto Gamefound's platform on October 16, 2025, its help center states 'Flexible Funding is no longer available for new campaigns,' so every new campaign is now all-or-nothing like Kickstarter, and new campaigns must pass a platform compliance review and a financial KYC check. Its backer article on cancelling a pledge states that during the crowdfunding phase a backer can cancel and won't be charged, but 'In the Pledge Manager phase, you have to contact the creator if you want to cancel your pledge'; refunds are issued by the creator from the creator's own order dashboard. None of the pages read describes a platform guarantee that a funded project delivers. The score moves from 28 to 30, level with Kickstarter, because the keep-what-you-raise option that left backers of unfunded campaigns exposed has been withdrawn. The FTC's 2020 settlement banning iBackPack creator Douglas Monahan, who raised over $800,000 on Indiegogo and Kickstarter and delivered nothing, ran against the campaigner, not the platform.

links.label: How to cancel a pledge in crowdfunding
What changed with the Platform Upgrade?
FTC: crowdfunding scheme operator banned from future crowdfunding

products.name: GoFundMe
products.description: A personal and community fundraising platform for medical bills, emergencies, memorials and causes, funded by cards and by an optional donor tip rather than a cut of the fundraiser itself.

fees.note: GoFundMe's pricing page states there is no fee to create or manage a fundraiser; a transaction fee of 2.9% + $0.30 applies per donation in the US, and donor tips, which support GoFundMe's operations, are optional and never required.

buyer_protection.note: The GoFundMe Giving Guarantee page states donations to an individual's fundraiser are covered for one full year against misuse of funds based on the fundraiser's stated purpose, or failure of funds to reach the beneficiary, with GoFundMe's Trust & Safety team investigating claims and refunds processed in 3 to 10 business days. The same page states the outcome is decided in GoFundMe's 'sole and absolute discretion' and that the guarantee is explicitly 'not a warranty against fraud or any other misuse of the Platform.'

accessibility.note: GoFundMe's help center states there are 20 countries where it can send funds and lists them by name, with a fundraiser's country locked in once created; donors, by contrast, are not limited to those countries when giving by card.

products.name: DonorsChoose
products.description: Lets donors fund specific project requests from US public school teachers. DonorsChoose buys and ships the requested books, supplies or equipment itself once a project is funded, rather than handing cash to the teacher.

fees.note: DonorsChoose's help center states a third-party payment processing fee of 1.5% of the project cost is added to every project, plus a flat Fulfillment labor & materials fee of $30.00 that covers the labor to bring a project to life and the physical costs of processing student thank-you letters. A separate 15% donation to DonorsChoose is suggested at checkout but is not required. On a typical few-hundred-dollar classroom project, the flat $30 fee alone is a meaningful share of the total.

buyer_protection.note: DonorsChoose's financials page states the organization purchases the requested classroom resources directly from the vendor and ships them to the school, rather than sending cash to the teacher, so a funded project's money cannot be redirected to anything other than the listed materials.

products.name: GlobalGiving
products.description: A crowdfunding marketplace for vetted nonprofit projects worldwide. Every listed organization goes through a due-diligence application before it can fundraise, and GlobalGiving keeps a support fee to help fund that vetting.

fees.note: GlobalGiving's help center states it retains a 5-12% nonprofit support fee, 5-7% for most donations, plus a 3% third-party processing fee on donations, and that this fee covers vetting costs and helps deliver additional matching and bonus funding to partner organizations.

buyer_protection.note: GlobalGiving's help center states it carefully vets every nonprofit before it can fundraise on the platform, requiring legal documentation and a compliance and due-diligence review, and conducts ongoing monitoring of reports, activity and community feedback afterward. The same article states plainly that 'no platform can guarantee outcomes.'

links.label: How can I be sure a project is legitimate?

products.name: Patreon
products.description: A recurring membership platform where supporters pay creators monthly or per piece of work for ongoing access, rather than backing a single time-bound campaign.

fees.note: Patreon's Creator fees overview states creators who publish a page after August 4, 2025 are on its standard plan, a 10% platform fee plus applicable taxes, plus payment processing of 2.9% + $0.30 per US credit card charge; creators who published on or before that date keep a legacy rate of 5%, 8% or 11% unless their page is unpublished and republished.

products.name: Experiment
products.description: An all-or-nothing crowdfunding platform for scientific research projects, reviewed by Experiment's team before they can list, with funds released only if a project reaches its goal.

fees.note: Experiment's FAQ states it is free to start a project, and if a project is fully funded, Experiment charges an 8% platform fee plus payment processing fees of roughly 3% to 5%.

buyer_protection.note: Experiment's FAQ states it is an all-or-nothing fundraising platform: if a project does not reach its goal, none of the backers are charged. The FAQ does not describe a guarantee or refund process for a project that is funded but does not deliver its stated research outcomes.

accessibility.note: Experiment's FAQ asks 'Who funds projects on Experiment?' and answers 'Everyone! ... it allows anyone with a credit card to bring real science to life,' while researcher eligibility to create a project is limited to the US, UK, Canada and Australia.

products.name: JustGiving
products.description: A UK online fundraising platform for registered charities and personal fundraising pages, charging no platform fee and covering its costs through payment processing charges and optional donor tips.

fees.note: JustGiving's fees page states it does not charge a platform fee and that it is free to set up a page. For UK charity fundraising it charges payment processing of 1.9% + £0.30 per donation on standard payment methods, rising to 2.9% + £0.35 per donation on personal and crowdfunding pages; donor tips are optional.

products.name: Givebutter
products.description: A US nonprofit fundraising and events platform that reaches 0% platform fees when donors opt to cover the cost with a tip, which most donors do.

fees.note: Givebutter's pricing page states nonprofits pay a 0% platform fee, and processing fees are also waived under the Givebutter Guarantee, when donor tips are enabled. If an organization disables tips instead, a flat 3% platform fee applies on top of standard processing of 2.9% + $0.30 for cards or 1.9% + $0.30 for ACH transfers.

products.name: FundRazr
products.description: A Vancouver-based fundraising platform for personal, nonprofit and community campaigns that pays organizers directly through their own Stripe or PayPal account rather than holding funds itself.

fees.note: FundRazr's pricing page states its Optional Tips model charges a 0% platform fee, with only the 2.9% + $0.30 payment processing fee applying and typically covered by donor tips; its alternative Fee Recovery model charges a 1% fee for donation forms or 5% for fundraising pages, plus processing.

buyer_protection.note: FundRazr's FAQ states plainly that FundRazr does not hold funds in escrow at all: money is transferred directly to the organizer's own Stripe or PayPal account, minus fees, immediately on contribution for keep-it-all campaigns, with no platform-level review of the transfer described.

products.name: Zeffy
products.description: A donation and event platform built specifically for nonprofits, funded entirely by an optional donor contribution at checkout, so a nonprofit's payout is never reduced by a platform or processing fee.

fees.note: Zeffy's help center states it offers its technology to nonprofits '100% free of charge' and covers all processing and platform costs itself; donors are given the option to make a voluntary contribution to Zeffy at checkout, and nonprofits receive 100% of every payment regardless of whether a donor adds one.

accessibility.note: Zeffy's help center states nonprofit accounts are only named for the US, Canada and the UK, but that 'Zeffy accepts credit card payments from individuals from almost anywhere in the world,' so giving is broader than the list of countries that can hold an account.

products.name: StartEngine
products.description: An SEC-registered funding portal for equity crowdfunding, where people invest in early-stage companies rather than donate to them, and where federal rules require committed funds to sit in escrow until a raise closes.

fees.note: StartEngine's investor FAQ states many offerings are completely free for investors because StartEngine charges fees to the company raising money instead. Where a fee does apply to investors, the FAQ states it is a 3.5% processing fee shown clearly on the investment form.

buyer_protection.note: SEC Regulation Crowdfunding requires a funding portal to direct investors to transmit money to a qualified third party, a registered broker-dealer or a bank, which holds the funds and transmits them to the company only once investment commitments reach the offering's target amount; an investor may cancel a commitment for any reason until 48 hours before the offering deadline. StartEngine's own investor FAQ confirms funds are withdrawn from an investor's account only once a company has exceeded its minimum funding goal and escrow has been opened.

accessibility.note: The SEC's investor bulletin on Regulation Crowdfunding states a non-accredited investor's annual limit is the greater of $2,500 or 5% of the greater of their annual income or net worth if either figure is below $124,000, rising to 10% of annual income or net worth, capped at $124,000 a year, once both figures are at or above that threshold. Giving through StartEngine means calculating and staying under one of these limits, unlike a straightforward donation.

links.label: SEC investor bulletin: Regulation Crowdfunding for investors

products.name: Wefunder
products.description: An SEC-registered funding portal for equity crowdfunding, run as a public benefit corporation, where people invest small amounts in early-stage companies rather than donate to them. Federal rules require committed money to sit with a bank or broker-dealer until a raise reaches its target.

fees.note: Wefunder's help center article 'What fees does Wefunder charge investors?' states it charges investors 'a transaction fee of 2% for payments made by bank ACH or wires', with an $8 minimum and a $150 maximum, while credit cards, Apple Pay and Google Pay cost 5.5% + $2 with no maximum cap per transaction, and the fee structure starts over if an investment is increased. Paying by bank keeps the cost below StartEngine's 3.5% investor fee; paying by card makes it higher, so the score sits just under StartEngine's.

buyer_protection.note: SEC Regulation Crowdfunding, 17 CFR 227.303(e), requires a funding portal to direct investors to send money to a qualified third party, a registered broker-dealer or an insured bank or credit union, that has agreed in writing to 'hold the funds for the benefit of' the investors, and to release it to the company only once commitments reach the offering's target and the cancellation period has passed, otherwise returning it. FINRA's list of the funding portals it regulates, updated September 29, 2026, includes Wefunder Portal LLC (SEC File No. 7-33), so the rule applies to Wefunder's Regulation Crowdfunding offerings. Scored level with StartEngine, which rests on the same rule; it protects the money until a raise closes, not the investment afterwards.

accessibility.note: The SEC's investor bulletin on Regulation Crowdfunding sets the same annual limits that apply to every US funding portal: a non-accredited investor whose annual income or net worth is below $124,000 can invest up to the greater of $2,500 or 5% of the greater of the two in any 12-month period, rising to 10%, capped at $124,000, once both are at or above that level. Backing a company here means working out and staying under that limit, unlike a straightforward donation; scored level with StartEngine, which sits under the same rule.

links.label: What fees does Wefunder charge investors?
SEC investor bulletin: Regulation Crowdfunding for investors

products.name: Republic
products.description: A US investment platform whose Regulation Crowdfunding offerings run through OpenDeal Portal LLC, an SEC-registered funding portal, letting non-accredited investors put small sums into startups, with committed money held by a bank or broker-dealer until a raise closes.

fees.note: Republic's investor help article on what fees Republic charges states that the administrative fee charged to investors is typically 2.5% with a minimum of $5 and a maximum cap of $250, though it may vary by offering, and that the fee is refunded only if an offering is canceled or withdrawn, not when an investor cancels a commitment. It applies to offerings hosted by OpenDeal Portal LLC and OpenDeal Broker LLC; Deal Room offerings for accredited investors can carry other fees. Scored level with StartEngine's 3.5% where charged, since the $250 cap keeps larger investments cheaper.

buyer_protection.note: SEC Regulation Crowdfunding, 17 CFR 227.303(e), requires a funding portal to have investors send money to a qualified third party, a registered broker-dealer or an insured bank or credit union, that agrees in writing to 'hold the funds for the benefit of' the investors, releasing it to the company only once commitments reach the target and the cancellation period has passed. FINRA's list of the funding portals it regulates, updated September 29, 2026, includes OpenDeal Portal LLC with 'Republic' as its other name and republic.com as its website. Scored level with StartEngine, which rests on the same rule.

accessibility.note: The SEC's investor bulletin on Regulation Crowdfunding sets the same annual limits that apply to every US funding portal: a non-accredited investor whose annual income or net worth is below $124,000 can invest up to the greater of $2,500 or 5% of the greater of the two in any 12-month period, rising to 10%, capped at $124,000, once both are at or above that level. Backing a company here means working out and staying under that limit, unlike a straightforward donation; scored level with StartEngine, which sits under the same rule.

links.label: SEC investor bulletin: Regulation Crowdfunding for investors

products.name: Republic Europe (formerly Seedrs)
products.description: The UK and European equity crowdfunding platform formerly called Seedrs, now part of Republic. It is run by Seedrs Limited, an FCA-authorised firm, and investors normally hold their shares through its nominee.

fees.note: Republic Europe's help article on investor fees (written November 20, 2025) states investors pay 2.5% when they first invest, minimum £/€5 and maximum £/€250, '0% periodic holding fees (no annual fees)', and, on a company exit, a 5% carry fee on any profit per investment; buying or selling on its secondary market costs 2%. Direct investment outside the nominee costs a one-off 2% (maximum £/€250) with no carry. It charges nothing for depositing, withdrawing, currency conversion or cancelling. The upfront fee is close to Republic's US fee; the carry on profits places it slightly below.

buyer_protection.note: The FCA's Financial Services Register lists Seedrs Limited (firm reference number 550317, website europe.republic.com) as authorised since 18 May 2012 and able to hold and control client money, and states that the Financial Ombudsman Service may consider a complaint and the FSCS may pay compensation if the firm goes out of business owing money, depending on the activity. It does not protect against a company failing. The same record shows a voluntary requirement the firm agreed on 23 March 2026 not to establish business relationships with any new high-risk customers. UK equity crowdfunding has no rule like the US escrow-until-target requirement. The score reflects regulated client-money handling and ombudsman access, lowered for the 2026 requirement.

accessibility.note: The FCA Handbook, COBS 4.12A, sets the conditions a UK platform must meet before a retail investor can respond to an offer of restricted mass market investments, which include non-readily realisable securities such as unlisted startup shares. The firm must allow 'a period of at least 24 hours' as a cooling-off period, give a personalised risk warning, have the investor certify a category (for example as a restricted investor, who agrees not to invest more than 10% of net assets in such investments), and assess that the investment is appropriate before processing the order. That paperwork comes before the first investment, comparable to the US Regulation Crowdfunding limits.

links.label: What fees does Republic Europe charge investors?
FCA Handbook COBS 4.12A: promotion of restricted mass market investments

products.name: Crowdcube
products.description: A UK equity crowdfunding platform run by Crowdcube Capital Limited, an FCA-authorised firm, where people invest in private companies rather than donate to them. Its own fee pages could not be opened for this check, so it carries no fee score.

buyer_protection.note: The FCA's Financial Services Register lists Crowdcube Capital Limited (firm reference number 650205, website www.crowdcube.com) as authorised since 28 May 2015 and able to hold and control client money, and states that the Financial Ombudsman Service may consider a complaint and the FSCS may pay compensation if the firm goes out of business owing money, depending on the activity; neither covers a company that fails. UK equity crowdfunding has no rule like the US escrow-until-target requirement, so the score sits well below the US funding portals and reflects regulated client-money handling and ombudsman access.

accessibility.note: The FCA Handbook, COBS 4.12A, requires a UK platform offering restricted mass market investments, which include non-readily realisable securities such as unlisted shares, to allow 'a period of at least 24 hours' as a cooling-off period, give a personalised risk warning, have the investor certify a category (a restricted investor agrees not to invest more than 10% of net assets in such investments) and assess appropriateness before processing a first order. The same paperwork applies on every UK equity platform.

links.label: FCA Handbook COBS 4.12A: promotion of restricted mass market investments

products.name: Gamefound
products.description: A reward-based crowdfunding and pledge-manager platform, and since 2025 the owner of Indiegogo, which now runs on its platform. Campaigns are all-or-nothing, and its backer terms add a refund right if a reward's price rises by more than 10% after the campaign.

fees.note: Gamefound's help center article on fees (last updated August 10, 2026) states 'Platform fee: we take 5% of the collected amount.' plus a fixed per-transaction processing fee, and gives the example of a $10,000 project paying a $500 platform fee and $320 in processing on 100 transactions for a $9,180 payout. If a project does not reach its goal, nothing is charged, including payment processing. The same structure as Indiegogo's, so the same score.

buyer_protection.note: Gamefound's Terms of Service for Backers state that Gamefound is not a store, that the creator alone is responsible for delivering rewards, and that backers agree to each creator's own refund and cancellation policy. Two additions go further than Kickstarter's terms: the creator guarantees a reward's price and estimated shipping will not rise by more than ten percent after the campaign, with a 100% refund available within 14 days if it does, and Gamefound may require a creator to refund affected backers or suspend the pledge manager. If a creator does not respond to a claim, a backer can ask Gamefound for operational help with dispute resolution. Scored a little above Kickstarter's 30.

links.label: Fees for projects funded on Gamefound

products.name: Ulule
products.description: A crowdfunding platform run by Paris-based Ulule SAS, registered in France as a crowdfunding intermediary, for creative, community and product projects, with all-or-nothing reward campaigns and a donation mode. Since April 2025, backers pay a small service fee on top of each contribution as well as the creator's commission.

fees.note: Ulule's terms (last updated December 17, 2025) set the creator's commission on reward campaigns at 'commission of 6.67% excl. VAT for funds collected by Credit Cards' on the first €100,000 (8% with 20% VAT), falling in tiers above that, charged only if the goal is reached; donation and subscription campaigns pay it on whatever is collected. Backers also pay 'service fees of 10 cents + 2.2% including VAT on the total amount of each Contribution', refunded if a reward campaign fails. Taken together, roughly 10% of a typical card contribution goes on fees, level with Patreon's standard plan.

buyer_protection.note: The same terms state that in reward mode a contribution is collected only if the goal is reached, that a creator who cannot deliver the promised rewards 'expressly commits to refunding them in full and accepts that the Company cannot assist him in this process', and that once funds are transferred a backer wanting a refund 'must then interact directly with the Creator'. Ulule can cancel a fundraiser and refund contributions if it identifies an undisclosed risk the creator does not correct within 48 hours. A written refund commitment from the creator, but no platform guarantee: scored just above Kickstarter.

products.name: Ko-fi
products.description: A platform where supporters tip creators, join memberships, buy from their shops or pay for commissions. Payments go straight to the creator's own PayPal or Stripe account rather than being held by Ko-fi.

fees.note: Ko-fi's pricing page states creating a page is free, that the Standard plan (the default for new creators) charges a 5% service fee on all payment types plus normal payment processor fees, that creators not opted in to Standard pay 0% on one-time tips, and that a $12-a-month Gold plan removes the service fee; it adds there are no buyer fees, payout fees or other surprises. At the default 5% plus processing, scored level with Kickstarter.

buyer_protection.note: The same pricing page states that on Ko-fi creators get paid directly and Ko-fi never holds their money, and that because Ko-fi does not process payments a creator must connect a PayPal or Stripe account; creators set their own prices and terms. With no platform escrow or guarantee, a supporter's recourse is the creator's own terms or a dispute with PayPal or their card issuer, the same position as FundRazr's direct payout.

accessibility.note: The pricing page lists the ways supporters can pay: PayPal, Apple Pay, Google Pay, Venmo, Cash App, credit and debit cards and popular local payment methods, with PayPal and Venmo depending on the creator having connected a PayPal account. A wide choice of everyday payment methods makes giving from most places straightforward.

products.name: Liberapay
products.description: An open, nonprofit-run platform for recurring donations to creators and open projects, based in France. It takes no cut of donations and is funded by donations to its own account.

fees.note: Liberapay's FAQ states 'Liberapay does not take a cut of payments', with the service funded by donations to its own account, so only payment processing fees apply; it reports that over the last year these averaged 3% for payments through Stripe and 5% through PayPal. Scored just below GoFundMe, which also takes no platform cut but has a lower card rate.

buyer_protection.note: The FAQ states that Liberapay is only for donations, which 'must not be linked to a contract nor a promise of recompense', that money goes immediately to the recipient's Stripe or PayPal account, and that stopping a donation cancels future renewals without any refund. Against impostors, it says a profile can be checked through the social accounts connected to it, which only the account holder can link. No promise exists to enforce, and nothing is held: scored level with FundRazr's direct payout.

accessibility.note: Liberapay's Global page states 'Donations can come from anywhere in the world.' and that donors can choose between up to 132 currencies, depending on the recipient and payment processor. The FAQ adds that paying through PayPal requires the donor to have or create a PayPal account, and caps giving at $100.00 per week to any one user.

products.name: Open Collective
products.description: A platform where groups such as open-source projects and community collectives raise and spend money in the open through a fiscal host, a legal entity that holds the funds and approves spending, in a platform built to collect and spend money transparently. Stewarded since October 2024 by a membership nonprofit.

fees.note: Open Collective's pricing page (updated for new organizations from March 2026) states that crowdfunding contributions are 'Free with Platform Tips activated', tips being optional and added on top of a contribution, or a host can opt for 'a simple 5% Crowdfunding Fee instead of tips'; Collectives themselves pay nothing. The fiscal host can charge its own hosting fee on top: the Open Source Collective host states on its application page that its fee is 10% of funds raised. With a 10% host fee plus card processing, a contribution loses about as much as on Patreon; under a host that charges less, more reaches the group.

buyer_protection.note: The same page states that Hosts receive and hold contributions on behalf of the Collectives they support and 'ensure that funds are used in line with their purpose and policies', and that Collectives do not hold funds directly; a host can charge hosting fees and runs antifraud checks and expense management. Money therefore passes through a legal entity that approves each expense before it is paid out, rather than straight to an individual, but no refund guarantee to contributors is described. Scored between GoFundMe's limited guarantee and GlobalGiving's vetting.

links.label: Open Source Collective: apply and fees
